What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the distributed version control tool that runs locally and tracks history. GitHub is a hosting platform for Git repositories that adds collaboration features: pull requests, code review, issues, branch protection, Actions CI/CD, packages and security scanning. GitLab and Bitbucket are alternatives offering similar features.
Explain the working tree, staging area and repository.

The working tree is your files on disk; the staging area (index) is the snapshot you are preparing for the next commit; the repository (.git) stores committed history. git add moves changes into the index and git commit records the index as a commit. Staging lets you commit only part of your changes (git add -p), keeping commits focused.
What is a branch in Git, really?

A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit — literally a file under .git/refs/heads containing a SHA. When you commit on a branch, the pointer moves to the new commit. HEAD is a pointer to the current branch. That is why branching is instant and cheap in Git, unlike SVN where a branch is a directory copy on the server.
git fetch vs git pull?

git fetch downloads new commits and updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main without touching your working branch. git pull is fetch followed by a merge (or a rebase with --rebase / pull.rebase=true) into the current branch. 💡 Fetching first lets you inspect incoming changes with git log HEAD..origin/main before integrating.
Merge vs rebase — when do you use each?

Merge preserves history exactly and adds a merge commit; it is safe for shared branches. Rebase rewrites your commits onto a new base for a linear history, ideal for updating a personal feature branch with the latest main before a PR. Never rebase commits that others have based work on, because it rewrites hashes; after rebasing a pushed feature branch, push with --force-with-lease.
How do you resolve a merge conflict?

Run git status to see conflicted files, open each and edit the region between <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> to the correct combined code, removing the markers. Then git add the file and run git merge --continue (or git rebase --continue). Build and run tests before pushing. Use an IDE merge tool for complex cases, and --abort to start over. 💡 Pulling main frequently keeps conflicts small.
git reset vs git revert?

git revert adds a new commit that inverts an earlier commit — history is preserved, so it is the right way to undo something already pushed to a shared branch. git reset moves the branch pointer backwards, effectively removing commits from the branch's history; it is for local, unpushed work. Resetting pushed commits forces everyone else to reconcile rewritten history.
Explain git reset --soft, --mixed and --hard.

All three move HEAD/the branch to the target commit. --soft leaves the undone changes staged; --mixed (the default) leaves them in the working tree but unstaged; --hard discards them from both index and working tree. Example: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but keeps the work ready to recommit. Lost commits after --hard can usually be recovered with git reflog.
What is git cherry-pick and when is it useful?

It applies the changes of one or more specific commits onto the current branch as new commits. Typical uses: back-porting a bug fix from main to a release or hotfix branch, or rescuing a commit made on the wrong branch. Overusing it duplicates commits across branches, which can confuse later merges; -x records the original commit hash in the message.
What is git stash?

It saves uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) onto a stack and cleans the working tree, so you can switch branches for an urgent fix. git stash pop reapplies the latest and removes it; apply keeps it; git stash list and git stash drop manage the stack; -u includes untracked files. For longer interruptions, a WIP commit on a branch is often safer.
Compare Git Flow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development.

Git Flow uses main + develop plus feature, release and hotfix branches — structured, suits versioned scheduled releases, but heavyweight. GitHub Flow uses short-lived feature branches off an always-deployable main merged via PRs. Trunk-based integrates small changes into main at least daily with feature flags hiding incomplete work, requiring strong CI and tests; it best supports continuous delivery. Choice depends on release cadence and team size.
What makes a good pull request and code review?

A good PR is small, single-purpose, has a descriptive title and summary (what and why), links the ticket, includes tests and passes CI. Reviewers look for correctness, edge cases, readability, naming, test coverage, security (input validation, secrets) and performance, giving specific, respectful comments and distinguishing blockers from suggestions. Branch protection enforces required approvals and green checks before merge.
Squash and merge vs rebase and merge vs merge commit?

Merge commit keeps all branch commits plus a merge commit — full history. Squash and merge combines the PR into a single commit on main — clean, one commit per feature, easy to revert, but loses granular commits. Rebase and merge replays each commit onto main linearly without a merge commit. Many teams use squash for feature PRs.
What is GitHub Actions? Describe a workflow.

GitHub's CI/CD platform. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows triggered by events like push or pull_request; it contains jobs that run on runners, and each job has steps that run commands or reusable actions. For a Java + Angular project, a workflow would check out code, set up JDK and Node with caching, run mvn verify and npm ci && npm run build, then optionally build a Docker image and deploy on merge to main. Secrets are injected from repository/environment settings.
A file is in .gitignore but Git still tracks it — why?

.gitignore only prevents untracked files from being added; files already committed stay tracked. Remove it from the index while keeping it on disk with git rm --cached path/to/file, commit, and it will be ignored from then on. If it contained secrets, rotate them — they remain in history unless it is rewritten.
What is the difference between Git and SVN?

Git is distributed: every clone has full history, so commits, branches, log and diff work offline and are fast; you commit locally and push later. SVN is centralised: the server holds history, svn commit goes straight to the server, and revisions are sequential numbers. Branching in Git is a cheap pointer, while SVN branches are directory copies under /branches. SVN offers file locking, path-level permissions and partial checkouts, which some teams with large binary assets prefer.
Explain SVN trunk, branches and tags, and the basic workflow.

By convention /trunk is the main development line, /branches holds feature or release lines and /tags holds read-only release snapshots — all created with svn copy. The daily workflow is svn checkout once, then svn update to get others' changes, edit, svn status/svn diff to review, and svn commit -m to publish. Conflicts are resolved during update and marked with svn resolve.
How do you undo a commit that was already pushed to main?

Use git revert <sha> (for a merge commit, git revert -m 1 <sha>) and push the new commit — this keeps shared history intact. Avoid git reset + force push on shared branches, since it breaks teammates' clones and is usually blocked by branch protection. 💡 If the change was a deployment issue, a revert PR goes through the normal CI pipeline, giving a traceable rollback.
You ran git reset --hard and lost commits. Can you get them back?

Yes, usually. git reflog records every position HEAD has been in, including commits no longer on any branch. Find the entry before the reset and run git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or create a branch at it. Reflog entries are local and expire (by default around 90 days for reachable, 30 for unreachable), and uncommitted changes discarded by --hard are not recoverable — commit or stash first.
How does git bisect work?

It binary-searches history between a known good and a known bad commit. You mark commits good or bad and Git checks out the midpoint each time, so 1,000 commits need about 10 steps. git bisect run <script> automates it: the script exits 0 for good and non-zero for bad (a failing test). Finish with git bisect reset.
How do you squash or edit commits before opening a PR?

Use interactive rebase: git rebase -i origin/main, then change pick to squash/fixup (combine), reword (edit message), edit (amend content) or drop. git commit --fixup=<sha> plus git rebase -i --autosquash automates the ordering. Only do this on your own branch, then git push --force-with-lease. For just the last commit, git commit --amend is enough.
A password was committed and pushed. What do you do?

First rotate/revoke the secret — assume it is compromised the moment it was pushed, because clones, forks and caches may already have it. Then remove it from history with git filter-repo (or BFG), force-push, and ask collaborators to re-clone; on GitHub, contact support to purge cached views if needed. Finally prevent a repeat: move the value to a secret manager or environment variable, add the file to .gitignore, and enable secret scanning or a pre-commit hook such as Gitleaks. 💡 A git revert alone is not enough — the secret is still in history.
What are Git hooks and how do you share them with a team?

Hooks are scripts Git runs at points like pre-commit, commit-msg and pre-push. The .git/hooks folder is not versioned, so teams use Husky (with lint-staged to lint only staged files) for Angular projects, or the pre-commit framework / a Maven plugin for Java. Typical checks: Prettier/ESLint, Spotless/Checkstyle, commit message format, quick unit tests. Hooks are a convenience; CI is the real gate because --no-verify skips them.
How do you keep a fork in sync with the original repository?

Add the original as a second remote: git remote add upstream <url>. Then git fetch upstream and either git rebase upstream/main (clean history on your feature branch) or merge it, and push to your fork (origin). Open PRs from your fork's branch to upstream's main. GitHub's "Sync fork" button does the same for the default branch.
Why do shell scripts fail in Docker after being committed from Windows?

They were checked out or committed with CRLF line endings, so Linux sees /bin/sh^M and fails with "bad interpreter" or "not found". Fix with a .gitattributes file (* text=auto, *.sh text eol=lf) and renormalise with git add --renormalize .. core.autocrlf is a per-machine setting, so .gitattributes is the reliable, versioned fix.
How does Git store data internally?

As immutable objects addressed by the hash of their content: blobs (file contents), trees (directories), commits (tree + parents + metadata) and annotated tags. Branches are refs — small files holding a commit hash — and HEAD points to the current branch. Because a commit hash covers its parent, changing any commit changes all descendants, which is why rebasing creates new commits and why pushed history should not be rewritten. Objects are compressed into packfiles to save space.
What is a signed commit and why would a team require it?

A signed commit carries a GPG, SSH or S/MIME signature (git commit -S) proving it was made by the holder of that key, since the author name and email in a commit can be set to anything. GitHub shows a "Verified" badge and branch protection can require signed commits. It is part of software supply-chain security alongside protected branches, required reviews and CODEOWNERS.
